findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: feat = close.shift(-1) / close - 1.0          # LEAK: t sees P[t+1]
findings.explanation: close.shift(-1) moves tomorrow's closing price into today's row, so feat at time t equals (P[t+1]/P[t] - 1). The position signal pos is therefore constructed entirely from a future price that would be unknown at decision time t, constituting a direct one-bar look-ahead bias.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace close.shift(-1) with close.shift(1) (or close.pct_change()) to use yesterday's close as the momentum input, ensuring the feature at time t is built only from prices available at or before t. Also remove the special-case iloc[-1] = 0 zeroing, which was only needed to mask the NaN introduced by the negative shift.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: scaler.fit(features)                 # LEAK: fitted before the split
findings.explanation: The custom Scaler is fitted on the entire `features` series (all 400 rows) before the train/test split is applied. Its `fit` method computes `mu` and `sd` from np.mean and np.std over the full sample (line 12), so both statistics incorporate values from the held-out test period (rows `split:` onward). When `transform` is subsequently called on the training slice (line 22) and the out-of-sample slice (line 23), both use a mean and standard deviation that have already seen future data, constituting direct look-ahead bias in the preprocessing step.
findings.suggested_fix: Fit the scaler exclusively on the training portion: call `scaler.fit(features.iloc[:split])` instead of `scaler.fit(features)`, then apply `scaler.transform` to both slices as before. This ensures the scaling statistics are derived only from information available up to the split point.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: model.fit(x_test, resp_test)     # LEAK: fitted on the test slice
findings.explanation: The Ridge model is fitted on x_test and resp_test (the held-out slice) rather than on the training data. The subsequent prediction and error calculation are therefore entirely in-sample: the model has already seen every response value it is evaluated against, making the reported MSE an in-sample metric falsely presented as out-of-sample performance.
findings.suggested_fix: Fit the model on the training data and evaluate on the test data: replace `model.fit(x_test, resp_test)` with `model.fit(x_train, resp_train)`. The error should then be computed as `model.predict(x_test) - np.asarray(resp_test)`, which remains correct.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: z = (close - close.mean()) / close.std()   # LEAK: full-sample statistics
findings.explanation: close.mean() and close.std() are computed over the entire series before any position is taken. Every bar's z-score therefore incorporates price levels and volatility from all future bars, giving the strategy look-ahead information at every time step.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the whole-sample statistics with an expanding (or rolling) window computed only on past data, e.g.: rolling_mean = close.expanding().mean(); rolling_std = close.expanding().std(); z = (close - rolling_mean) / rolling_std. This ensures that at bar t only information from bars 0..t is used.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: edge = target.rolling(5).mean()           # LEAK: feature reads label values
findings.explanation: The feature 'edge' is computed as a rolling mean of 'target', which is itself the forward return (close.pct_change().shift(-1)). Each value of 'edge' at time t is the average of forward returns at t, t+1, t+2, t+3, and t+4 — all of which are future quantities relative to the decision point at t. This directly encodes future label information into a training feature, constituting a textbook label-leakage pattern.
findings.suggested_fix: Derive 'edge' from past returns only, not from the forward-return label. For example: past_ret = close.pct_change(); edge = past_ret.rolling(5).mean(). This uses only historically available data at each time step.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: px = raw.fillna(method="bfill")           # LEAK 1: gaps take future values
findings.explanation: fillna(method='bfill') propagates future prices backward: a NaN at time t is filled with the next available price at t+k (k>0), so the cleaned series at time t contains information that was not yet available at t.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace bfill with forward-fill: px = raw.fillna(method='ffill'). This fills gaps with the most recent known price rather than a future one.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: sig = close.shift(-2)                     # LEAK 2: t sees P[t+2]
findings.explanation: close.shift(-2) shifts the price series two steps into the future, so the signal at time t equals P[t+2], giving the strategy perfect knowledge of prices two periods ahead before any position is taken.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a non-negative shift (e.g., close.shift(1)) so the signal at time t is based only on prices known at or before t.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.explanation: close.groupby(day).transform('mean') computes the mean of every bar within the same calendar day and broadcasts it back to each bar in that day. A morning bar at 09:30 therefore receives a statistic that incorporates all afternoon prices from the same session — prices that do not yet exist at decision time. The relative-deviation 'rel' and the resulting position 'pos' are thus contaminated with future intraday information for every bar except the last one of each day.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the full-day mean with an expanding or rolling mean that is strictly backward-looking, e.g. use a groupby-cumsum approach: day_mean = close.groupby(day).expanding().mean().droplevel(0).sort_index(). This gives each bar only the average of prices up to and including that bar within the session, eliminating the look-ahead.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: drift = prices[t + horizon] / prices[t] - 1.0   # LEAK: reads the future
findings.explanation: At each bar t, `prices[t + horizon]` directly reads the closing price 5 bars in the future. This value is used to compute `drift` and set `pos[t]`, meaning the position held at time t is determined by information that is not yet available at t. This is a plain index look-ahead with no syntactic marker (no shift, no rolling, no bfill), making it invisible to rule-based scanners.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute drift using only information available at or before t. For a momentum-style signal use past returns, e.g. `drift = prices[t] / prices[t - horizon] - 1.0` (with t >= horizon as the loop guard), so the position at t is based solely on the price history up to and including t.

findings.title: Semantic leakage (LLM, to verify)
findings.snippet: pos[t] = 1.0 if z > k else (-1.0 if z < -k else 0.0)
findings.explanation: The signal at bar t is computed from prices[t] (the close of bar t) and immediately written into pos[t]. Whether this constitutes look-ahead bias depends entirely on how the external engine maps pos[t] to a trade: if it fills the position using bar-t's close or any intra-bar price, future information is consumed; if it defers execution to bar t+1, the logic is causal.
findings.suggested_fix: If the engine executes pos[t] at bar t's close (or any bar-t price), shift the output series by one period before passing it to the engine: `return pd.Series(pos, index=close.index, name='position').shift(1)`. If the engine already defers execution to bar t+1, no change is needed.
findings.external_dependency: Verify whether the consuming backtesting engine interprets pos[t] as a position entered at the close of bar t (look-ahead) or at the open/close of bar t+1 (causal); if the engine trades on the same bar whose close was used to compute the signal, there is look-ahead bias.
